html:
The main highway of Tokugawa Japan, running about 500 kilometres along the Pacific coast between Edo (Tokyo) and Kyoto. It was the busiest road in the country.

An older coastal route existed, but Tokugawa Ieyasu began to organise it as one of the Five Routes in 1601. Along it were 53 post stations with inns, horses and porters, starting from the Nihonbashi bridge in Edo. Guards at checkpoints, such as Hakone, watched for guns going in and lords' wives going out.

The road carried officials, merchants, pilgrims and, above all, the processions of lords travelling to and from Edo under the alternate attendance system. All this traffic spread goods, money and city culture through the provinces.

Hiroshige's print series The Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, from the 1830s, made its scenes famous. Hokusai drew it too. Modern Japan's main railway, and later the first Shinkansen line, follow much the same route.
